newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate visitors see smooth Hong Kong takeover.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate visitors see smooth Hong Kong takeover.

text.p: Two U.S. senators have found reasons for optimism when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1 next year -- an issue in which Congress has a special interest.
Senate Democratic Leader Thomas Daschle and Democratic Senator John Glenn of Ohio visited the British colony and talked to officials during a recently concluded Asia trip.

"China insists that it's going to be peaceful, insists that it's going to continue with the same system there, and we all hope that is right, of course," Glenn told reporters on Monday. "I personally am optimistic about that one because I think it's to China's advantage."
Daschle said people in Hong Kong "are quite optimistic about the prospects of a smooth transition, optimistic about the prospect for continued economic vitality and success."

Daschle said this was the prevalent view among U.S. embassy, government and business officials, adding he was impressed by the optimism of American businesses represented in Hong Kong, which he said "are continuing to invest accordingly."

Under the 1992 United States-Hong Kong Policy Act, Congress called for an active U.S. role in maintaining Hong Kong's confidence and prosperity, it's role as an international financial center and beneficial ties between the two peoples after Chinese resumption of sovereignty.

It said that unless changes were made, the laws of the United States "shall continue to apply with respect to Hong Kong" in the same way as they did before July 1 and treaties should continue in effect unless terminated.
In non-binding language, it said the United States should continue to fulfill its obligations to Hong Kong under international agreements regardless of whether the Beijing government was a party.

The law also said the United States should seek to maintain and expand economic and trade relations with Hong Kong and continue to treat it as a separate territory in economic and trade matters, such as import quotas and certificates of origin.
Under the law, the administration has to report to Congress annually on conditions in Hong Kong until the year 2000.
